0: no alert. An alert is a file in /var/db/os-useridentity/alerts, in os-xgs-npu's form, for os-netreport to send; the directory failing and an address newly shared are alerted too.
A group's name or distinguished name, on one line.

A table for each group: the addresses of its users, asked of the directory chosen in Settings when a user is first seen and again after 15 minutes. Each is an External alias in Firewall: Aliases, for a rule's source or destination. Changes here take effect with Apply.
A user in a group that is inside a chosen group counts as in it: Active Directory is asked by its in-chain rule, one question a group. A server that does not know the rule is asked memberOf alone.
A user's logon name, as the domain writes it.

Addresses and networks never mapped to a user: terminal servers, NAT inside the network, servers that log on to the domain controllers as a user. The firewall's own addresses and the domain controllers' never are.

An event older than this when it arrives neither maps nor renews: NXLog CE sends again what it held while stopped. Counted as stale on Sources. The events' times are read in the firewall's time zone: the domain controllers must keep the same zone, and a close clock.

Each address with the user a source last saw on it: a domain controller, RADIUS accounting or the captive portal. The latest wins: an address another user was seen on within the lifetime is shown as shared - a terminal server, or a runas on a client while someone sits at its screen - and as a clash when two sources gave it to two users. A RADIUS Stop and the end of a portal session end a mapping at once; a domain controller says nothing at a logoff: its mappings end at the end of their lifetime, when another device takes the address, or when forgotten here.
Each mapping made, changed or ended, kept a file a day in /var/db/os-useridentity/history for this many days. 0: none is kept, only the live map.

Every address is taken out of the map and of the tables now. The next logon or network logon of each user maps it again; a captive portal session still open within half a minute, a RADIUS session at its next Interim-Update.

Every minute, an address whose MAC in the firewall's ARP or neighbour table is not the one it had leaves the map: another device has it. Behind a router the firewall sees no MAC, and only the lifetime ends a mapping.

How long an address stays mapped with no event about it. A domain controller says nothing when a user logs off or locks the screen, so this is what ends a mapping, besides another user's logon from the same address. An idle session renews itself: the network logons it makes keep coming.
IPv4 addresses of domain controllers, one each.

Map each address to its user - from the domain controllers' logon events, RADIUS accounting and the captive portal's sessions, as chosen here - and fill the tables of the group and user rows. Off by default: nothing is mapped until a source is chosen and groups or users are named. Off, every mapping is forgotten and the plugin's aliases leave Firewall: Aliases - switched off instead where a rule or a setting still names one.

Map the address of each RADIUS session to its user, from the accounting os-freeradius writes as each request comes: a Start maps its Framed-IP-Address, an Interim-Update renews it, a Stop takes it out. A NAS - or another RADIUS server that forwards its accounting - must be a client of Services: FreeRADIUS. A NAS that sends no Interim-Update leaves the mapping to the end of its lifetime, even while the session goes on.

Map the address of each session of the captive portal to the user that logged on, from the logon to the logout or the portal's own timeout - read every two seconds from the portal's database. The sessions of allowed addresses, of vouchers and of zones with no login map nothing.
NXLog CE on each domain controller

NXLog Community Edition reads the Security log and sends the two events as JSON over TCP. Its configuration, as phase 0's lab ran it, to put in nxlog.conf on each domain controller named in Settings, then restart its service:
Not receiving: syslog-ng's source is not written.

RADIUS: each client of os-freeradius whose accounting was read - its records, the addresses a Start or an Interim-Update mapped or renewed, those a Stop ended, those older than the mapping lifetime when read (stale), those refused and why; Accounting-On and Accounting-Off, which end every session of their NAS, among the others. Captive Portal: each zone switched on - the sessions it held, the addresses they mapped and those their end took out, and those refused and why.

Since the collector started: the lines each sender sent, the events taken - a ticket issued (4768) or a logon to the domain controller with an address (4624) - those that mapped an address or renewed one, those older than Stale after when they came, those refused and why, and the other events counted and set aside. Late: how long after it happened the last event came. Lines are counted, never kept.

The IPv4 addresses of the domain controllers that send their logon events, with NXLog CE (Sources shows its configuration). Only these are let in: pf redirects their port to syslog-ng on 127.0.0.1, and a line from any other address is never read.

The LDAP entry of System: Access: Servers asked which groups a user is in. Active Directory refuses a bind in the clear: StartTLS or SSL, with the domain's certificate authority in System: Trust and the domain controller named as its certificate names it.

The TCP port the domain controllers send to, on the firewall's addresses. Not one the firewall itself serves - SSH, DNS, the web GUI on 80, 443 or its own port: the domain controllers would no longer reach that service.

The domain controllers keep their audit of Kerberos Authentication Service and of Logon for success, as Windows Server does by default. TLS from the domain controllers is not taken yet: the redirect, from their addresses alone, is what lets a line in.
The firewall itself serves this port (SSH, DNS or the web GUI): the domain controllers would no longer reach that service on it. Choose another, such as 514.
The group's name in the directory, or its distinguished name. A user in it - or, with Nested groups, in a group inside it - has its addresses in this row's table.

The port of syslog-ng's source on 127.0.0.1 that the domain controllers' lines are redirected to; 5140 is os-xgs-npu's. It is written only when no other program holds it: a source that cannot be bound would stop syslog-ng, and every log with it.
The system log says how many addresses were mapped, changed user or left. On, it names each address and its user, and so do the alerts.

integer($EventTime) / 1000000 makes NXLog CE send the time of each event as seconds since 1970, in UTC, so the firewall reads it right whatever the time zone of the domain controller; without it the time is read in the zone of the firewall. delete($Message) leaves out the long text of each event, which nothing here reads, and keeps each line well under what one datagram to the collector can carry.
